newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway central bank chief worried about inflation.
newsitem.headline: Norway central bank chief worried about inflation.

text.p: Norwegian central bank governor Kjell Storvik said on Wednesday fresh economic forecasts pointed to continued moderate price inflation, but said there was still a risk of an acceleration in price and wage inflation.
The central bank said it projected consumer price inflation at 2.75 percent to 3.0 percent in 1997, depending on future movements in the crown exchange rate.
The upward adjustment from 2.5 percent in the December inflation report primarily reflects higher indirect taxes, a statement said.
The rise in prices for 1998 was estimated at 2.0 percent to 2.5 percent.
"If our projections prove to be right, consumption growth will reach nine percent between 1995 and 1997," Storvik said in a statement accompanying the quarterly forecast on key economic indicators.
"Such rates have not been seen since the previous cyclical boom in 1985-1986. The sharp rise in house prices is also highly reminiscent of developments in the mid-1980s.

"Fiscal policies must assume responsibility for stabilising the economy. Monetary policy is oriented towards returning the crown exchange rate as defined in the exchange rate regulation," he said, reiterating official policy.

Price inflation, excluding indirect taxes and electricity prices, was projected at 2.0 to 2.25 percent in 1997 and 2.0 to 2.5 percent in 1998. Wage growth was estimated at 4.5 to 4.75 percent in 1997 and 5.0 to 5.5 percent in 1998.
Overall gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 1997 was upgraded to 4.25 percent from 3.5 percent three months ago. It was seen at 3.25 percent next year.
Mainland GDP, which excludes the booming offshore oil and gas sector, was projected to grow 3.25 percent this year, up from a lower forecast of 3.0 percent in the previous report.
Mainland GDP was seen at 2.75 percent in 1998.
